title: Federal and State Officials Ramp Up Scrutiny of DraftKings, Other Sports Betting Apps
author: Jake Pearson
content:
State and federal officials have ramped up scrutiny of online sports betting
companies in recent weeks, launching inquiries, demanding information and, in
one case, proposing a new rule that would limit when companies like DraftKings
can pitch their users to bet more.

The moves — by gaming regulators, government lawyers and federal lawmakers —
follow an investigation last month by ProPublica that tested the guardrails
DraftKings and other sports betting companies have in place to protect users
from spiraling out of control. That system is called responsible gaming, and
executives say it’s integral to their companies’ long-term success.

The ProPublica article showed how [DraftKings bestowed VIP status on a
reporter who deliberately bet like a problem
gambler](https://www.propublica.org/article/draftkings-sports-gambling-
problem-vip-fanduel). The report detailed the ways in which the app’s user
design and promotions encouraged more betting — even after the reporter opted
into responsible gaming tools designed to slow users down. A week earlier, The
New York Times reported that DraftKings had [used machine learning and
artificial intelligence to target promotions to losing
bettors](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/19/business/draftkings-ai.html).

Those articles were the focus of an [Oct. 15 meeting of the Louisiana Gaming
Control
Board](https://house.louisiana.gov/H_Video/VideoArchivePlayer?v=house/2026/Oct/1015_26_gcb),
which, partly in response to the stories, tabled the renewal of DraftKings’
five-year license. Instead, the board granted the company a temporary four-
month permit while investigators look into the issues raised in the reports as
well as other paperwork concerns.

The board’s chair, Christopher Hebert, said the Times had raised some “very
serious questions” and called ProPublica’s reporting “very troubling.”

While news stories “are not findings of regulatory violations,” Hebert said,
“as regulators we have a responsibility to examine these matters that could
affect the integrity of gaming operations and the protections of our citizens
here in Louisiana.”

State health officials say the number of Louisianans believed to have a
gambling disorder has risen in recent years amid the surge in popularity of
online gambling and prediction market sites. One top official reported this
summer that [gambling addiction was among the health department’s “top three
priorities.”](https://wgno.com/news/louisiana/is-problem-gambling-rising-in-
louisiana-as-sports-betting-prediction-markets-grow-popular/?nxsparam=5)

## [What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find
Out.](https://projects.propublica.org/sports-betting-uploader)

If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica
understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your
betting history, then upload your files.

[Share Your Experience](https://projects.propublica.org/sports-betting-
uploader)

Paul Liberman, who co-founded DraftKings and serves as its president of
operations, told the regulators: “We do not use artificial intelligence to
target losing gamblers by any means.”

DraftKings previously told ProPublica that it proactively closes the accounts
of suspected problem gamblers “all the time” but declined to provide specific
figures. Yet when asked by a Louisiana board member for those same specifics,
Lori Kalani, DraftKings’ chief responsible gaming officer, said 175 accounts
in the state had been shut down this year. She told the board she didn’t know
how many total users DraftKings had in the Pelican State.

“We’re not physicians, we’re not clinicians and that’s not our role, but we
certainly want to help people enjoy the service, the platform that we’re
offering them,” Kalani told the board. “I know that we’re doing our job and
that when we see something, we say something and we engage. I just can’t tell
you if 175 is the right number. I wish it was zero.”

In a statement, a DraftKings spokesperson said: “As a legal, regulated
operator, DraftKings values an open and ongoing dialogue with regulators and
regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of
business.”

In response to ProPublica’s original investigation, Kalani said DraftKings’
responsible gaming system — which consists largely of in-app messages about
the company’s tools — “worked the way it was supposed to.” She cautioned
against “drawing broad conclusions” from one user’s experience.

The day after the Louisiana meeting, regulators in Ohio proposed an amendment
to the state’s sports gaming rule that would [bar companies like DraftKings
from sending direct ads or
marketing](https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/v1792155478/casinocontrol.ohio.gov/csi/2026/Summary_of_Proposed_Changes_10.26.pdf)
to bettors for 48 hours after they’d opted into responsible gaming tools or
updated their current settings.

The proposed amendment speaks directly to a finding in ProPublica’s reporting:
After blowing nearly $4,500 betting on tennis in 24 hours, the reporter used
such tools to limit the amount of time and money he could spend on the app.
Just 30 minutes later, though, he received the first of four push
notifications promoting new betting opportunities. It wasn’t until he opted
into a far more restrictive tool, called a “cool-off,” that the notifications
temporarily stopped.

Andromeda Morrison, the interim executive director of the Ohio Casino Control
Commission, said that though her office had been working on its proposal for
some time, ProPublica’s story illuminated the issue. “Hopefully this is
something that is fairly easy for the industry to see as a common sense
restriction to make sure those consumers are making good choices without those
push notifications,” she said.

But Keith Whyte, a former director of the National Council on Problem Gambling
who now consults for industry and nonprofit groups, said the proposed
amendment could unintentionally disincentivize users from using tools like
deposit limits. “I think the implication is that using a responsible gaming
tool is a sign of a gambling problem,” he said. The measure faces a long
rulemaking process, including more rounds of public hearings and comments.

Sports betting operators are also feeling the heat at the federal level.

Citing ProPublica’s reporting, three Democrats who have long called for
industry reforms are now demanding more information from major sports betting
and prediction market companies about how the businesses entice their
customers.

The letters are signed by Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, New York Rep.
Paul Tonko and North Carolina Rep. Valerie Foushee. They asked the companies
to answer a series of questions, including how many customers are enrolled in
their VIP programs and how much revenue is generated by them.

“As repeated stories from exploited gamblers and media reports have vividly
documented, VIP programs are driving the gambling industry’s most susceptible
customers into debt and addiction through rewards tied to waging ever
increasing amounts of money,” the lawmakers wrote.

DraftKings conferred VIP status on a ProPublica reporter after he lost close
to $6,000 in three weeks on the app by chasing losses with long-shot bets,
playing late into the night and firing risky wagers on fast action, like
whether a major league baseball player will take a strike, a ball or connect
for a hit — betting behavior that experts say are clear red flags of problem
gambling.

In a statement, DraftKings said it would “respond accordingly once we have had
a chance to review” the letter. Its biggest competitor, FanDuel, which has
been trading letters with the lawmakers for months, wrote on Oct. 20 that the
company was committed to responsible gaming and said “the VIP program is
intended to provide enhanced service and encourage customers who chose to
wager to use FanDuel rather than another platform.”

The companies are likely to face further scrutiny.

In New York, investigators for the state’s attorney general have [contacted
former DraftKings
employees](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/26/business/draftkings-new-york-
louisiana-blumenthal.html) about issues raised in the Times’ story, the
newspaper reported, citing people familiar with the probe and messages it had
reviewed. A spokesperson for the office declined to comment.

That inquiry follows proposals earlier this month by state gaming officials
that they say will strengthen New York’s own standards governing the use of
[artificial intelligence and responsible gaming
guidelines](https://www.propublica.org/article/new-york-gaming-commission-
sports-betting-regulation).

Regulators in [Maine](https://wgme.com/news/i-team/maine-regulators-
monitoring-ai-use-by-sports-betting-apps-after-draftkings-allegations),
Massachusetts and
[Michigan](https://www.legalsportsreport.com/279553/michigan-regulators-
reviewing-issues-raised-in-draftkings-ai-vip-reports/) have also said that
they’re reviewing some of those same issues.

DraftKings, the spokesperson said, “does not market to customers based on
indicators of potential problem gaming.”

Still, there are signs that yet more states may be interested in vetting those
claims.

Jennifer Davenport, New Jersey’s attorney general, recently [told the RG
Journal, a publication that focuses on responsible gaming and industry
matters](https://rgjournal.com/do-no-harm-new-jersey-strengthens-responsible-
gaming-
regulations/?utm_source=rgjournal.beehiiv.com&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=responsible-
gaming-journal-
october-23-2026&_bhlid=32f20f3b6233c3ce4b3989158f45b2a136aad0b0), that “we are
monitoring recent press reports alleging certain sports books are ignoring our
consumer safeguards and chasing customers who are clearly exhibiting signs of
problem betting.”

“Let them be warned, our office stands ready to take action against anyone who
violates our gaming regulations and tries taking advantage of New Jerseyans
and those who gamble here,” she said.

A spokesperson for Davenport declined to comment.
